Estimate a population mean

Source: R/estimate.R
ht_mean.Rd

The Hajek estimator, sum(y / pi) / sum(1 / pi), is the default. It divides by the estimated population size rather than the known one, so a sample that happens to over-represent heavy-weight rows inflates numerator and denominator together and they partly cancel. estimator = "ht" divides by the true N instead.

Usage

ht_mean(
  sample,
  y,
  estimator = c("hajek", "ht"),
  variance = c("auto", "analytic", "jackknife", "none"),
  level = 0.95,
  by = NULL,
  df = NULL,
  proportion = NULL,
  ci_method = c("logit", "beta"),
  alternative = c("two.sided", "less", "greater"),
  contrast = NULL,
  na_rm = FALSE
)

Arguments

sample

A data frame returned by draw() with weights = TRUE. It is read as ht_total() reads it: .prob for the probabilities, and the stored frame for the design's columns. See "Which columns are read" there.

y

The variable to average: a column name, several column names, a numeric vector as long as sample, or a single number, which stands for that value in every row. A factor or character column, or a factor as long as sample, gives the share of each level. See "Several variables" and "Categories" in ht_total().

estimator

"hajek" or "ht". See above.

variance, level, by, df, alternative, contrast

As for ht_total().

proportion

Whether y is a proportion, which decides the shape of the interval. NULL decides from y: a logical y, or a column of the frame whose values are all 0 or 1, is a proportion, and a numeric vector or a column added after the draw is one when it is 0 or 1 in every sampled row. TRUE treats y as one, and needs it to be 0 or 1 in every sampled row; FALSE gives the symmetric interval. See "Proportions".

ci_method

The interval for a proportion: "logit", or "beta" for Korn and Graubard's. A proportion of exactly 0 or 1 gets "beta" either way. See "Proportions".

na_rm

FALSE refuses a missing y. TRUE estimates the mean over the rows with y present, as a domain of the sample. See "Missing values".

Value

A list with a print() method, holding mean, estimator, variable, variance, se, ci, level, alternative, df, n, n_random, design, deff, method, note, ci_scale ("linear", "logit" or "beta"), unreachable and n_missing, the sampled rows with y missing that na_rm = TRUE left out. See ht_total() for what variable, n_random, method, df, note and unreachable say, and deff() for the design effect. With by, a data frame with one row per domain, and with contrast a drawn_contrast, as for ht_total(). With several column names as y, a drawn_by table with a row per variable, and with a factor or character y one with a row per level, as for ht_total(). Each has coef(), vcov(), confint(), as.data.frame() and tidy() methods; see "Working with the result" in ht_total().

Proportions

For a 0/1 or logical variable either one estimates a proportion, and the confidence interval is then formed on the logit scale and transformed back (Korn and Graubard 1999, section 5.3). A symmetric interval around a small proportion runs below zero; this one cannot, and matches survey::svyciprop(method = "xlogit").

Whether y is a proportion is read from what y is, not from the values the sample happened to draw. A logical y is one, and so is a column of the frame whose values are all 0 or 1. A count that came out 0 or 1 in every sampled row is not: a logit interval cannot pass 1, so it would never cover a mean of 1.2. A numeric vector, or a column added to the sample after the draw, such as a 0/1 result recorded in fieldwork, has no column of the frame to read. It is taken for a proportion when it is 0 or 1 in every sampled row, and note says the choice came from the sample. proportion = FALSE asks for the symmetric interval whatever y is, and is the choice for a count.

ci_method = "beta" gives the Korn and Graubard (1998) interval instead, a Clopper-Pearson interval at an effective sample size of p(1 - p) / v, with p the estimate and v its variance, capped at n and then scaled by (qt(a, n - 1) / qt(a, df))^2 for the design's degrees of freedom. Here n is the number of sampled rows below certainty behind the estimate and a the tail probability of the interval. The scaled size is capped at n too, so a domain whose design has more degrees of freedom than the domain has rows gets no narrower an interval than Clopper-Pearson's over those rows. With no rows taken with certainty it matches survey::svyciprop(method = "beta") whenever neither cap binds. It ignores the finite population correction, so it errs wide when the sample is a large share of the frame.

An estimate of exactly 0 or 1, such as no deviations found in 60 sampled invoices, has a variance of 0, and a logit interval around it has no width. It gets the beta interval whatever ci_method says, with the effective sample size set to n, and note says so. For 0 of 60 from a simple random sample, the 95% upper bound (alternative = "less") is 4.87%. The interval needs no variance, so a design that leaves 0 degrees of freedom, such as a Poisson sample of one row, gets Clopper-Pearson's over the sampled rows. When every sampled row behind the estimate was taken with certainty, the estimate is exact and the interval has no width.

When the two differ, and which to use

They coincide exactly whenever the design weights of the rows you drew sum to N — which covers every fixed-size equal-probability design that can reach every row of the frame, and every design_stratified() without replacement that draws from every stratum, because each stratum contributes n_h * N_h / n_h = N_h. There is nothing to choose between them there. A design_spatial() sample from a region, or a design_reservoir() sample whose stream ran past max_items, is a simple random sample of the rows it can reach, and its weights sum to their number instead; see the caveat on "ht" below.

They differ when that sum is random or uneven:

  • the sample size itself is random — design_weighted() with method = "poisson", design_cluster() over clusters of unequal size, or design_systematic() with an interval that does not divide N;

  • the weights vary within a fixed-size sample — probability-proportional-to- size selection.

Hajek is usually the steadier of the two and is the default for that reason (Särndal, Swensson and Wretman 1992, section 5.7). The exception is worth knowing: when y is close to proportional to the size measure that drove selection, y / pi is nearly constant, the Horvitz-Thompson numerator barely moves, and dividing it by the known N beats dividing by an estimate. The Hajek mean's ratio bias, and a variance estimate that runs 11 to 12% low, also lower the coverage of its interval there. Drawing with n = 30 from 240 rows by Poisson PPS, its 95% interval covered 91% of the time and that of "ht" 94%. By systematic PPS both covered about 90%. "Confidence intervals" in ht_total() gives the figures and the reasons.

One caveat on "ht". It is unbiased for the frame mean provided every row could have been selected. Rows with inclusion probability 0, such as rows outside a time window or a region, past max_items or dropped under na_rm = TRUE, sit inside the N it divides by but can never enter the numerator, so the estimate is biased low by exactly their share of the frame. sample_summary() reports how many such rows there are. The Hajek mean is unaffected, because it estimates the mean of the part of the frame the design can actually reach.

Variance and domains

The Hajek mean is a ratio, and its variance is the variance of the total of the linearised residuals (y - mean) / N_hat (Deville 1999), computed with whichever estimator suits the design — see ht_total(), which also explains the confidence interval's degrees of freedom, how by estimates domain means from the whole sample rather than a subset of it, and what an empty sample gives.

The residuals sum to zero inside a primary sampling unit that holds every sampled row of the domain, so a Hajek mean over one unit, such as a domain with one sampled row or a Poisson sample of one row, gets no standard error. The "Domains" section of ht_total() says more.

With estimator = "ht" each domain's total is divided by the domain's number of rows in the frame, read from the frame's by columns. A frame row with a by value missing could be in any domain, so such a frame is refused.

contrast gives a weighted sum of domain means, such as the difference between two, with its standard error; see "Contrasts" in ht_total(). Its interval is symmetric whatever proportion and ci_method say.

When y has the same value in every sampled row, the residuals are 0 and the Hajek mean's variance is set to exactly 0, with a note, rather than left to rounding error, which gave standard errors near 1e-16 and design effects that changed from seed to seed. The design effect is then NA.

Shares and counts of categories

A factor or character column named as y, or a factor as long as sample, gives the share of each of its levels: a drawn_by table led by a level column, with a proportion's interval for each level and the covariances between the shares in vcov(). ht_total() gives the estimated number of frame rows at each level the same way; see "Categories" there. The share of one level is also the mean of its indicator, ht_mean(s, s$habitat == "forest"), which takes contrast as any y does.

A single number as y stands for that value in every row, so ht_total(s, 1) estimates the number of frame rows the design can reach, and ht_total(s, 1, by = "habitat") the number in each domain.

Missing values

A missing y is refused unless na_rm = TRUE. Then the mean is the Hajek mean over the rows with y present, treated as a domain of the whole sample, with the design's own variance estimator, and equals survey::svymean(na.rm = TRUE) on as_svydesign(). It assumes the values are missing completely at random, and the printed result says so. n counts the rows with y present, n_missing the others, and the design effect is NA, as for a domain. With by, each domain is the rows of its by values with y present. estimator = "ht" is refused, since the number of frame rows that would have a y is unknown. See "Missing values and nonresponse" in ht_total() for when the assumption fails and what to do then.

References

Korn, E. L. and Graubard, B. I. (1998). Confidence intervals for proportions with small expected number of positive counts estimated from survey data. Survey Methodology, 24, 193–201.

Korn, E. L. and Graubard, B. I. (1999). Analysis of Health Surveys. Wiley. doi:10.1002/9781118032619

Hájek, J. (1971). Comment on "An essay on the logical foundations of survey sampling, part one" by D. Basu. In V. P. Godambe and D. A. Sprott (eds.), Foundations of Statistical Inference, p. 236. Holt, Rinehart and Winston.

Särndal, C.-E., Swensson, B. and Wretman, J. (1992). Model Assisted Survey Sampling. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4612-4378-6

Deville, J.-C. (1999). Variance estimation for complex statistics and estimators: linearization and residual techniques. Survey Methodology, 25, 193–203.

See also

ht_total(), ht_ratio(), ht_quantile(), deff(), sample_summary()

Examples

set.seed(1)
pop <- data.frame(
  id = 1:200,
  site = rep(c("a", "b"), times = c(150, 50)),
  spend = round(stats::runif(200, 10, 500))
)
s <- draw(pop, design_stratified("site", n = 40), seed = 1, weights = TRUE)

ht_mean(s, "spend")
#> Hajek mean  (stratified design, n = 40)
#>   estimate 270
#>   se       18.56849  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  232.4101 to 307.5899  (t, 38 df)
#>   deff     1.03  (about the same as simple random sampling)
mean(pop$spend)   # the truth
#> [1] 263.66

# A mean for each site, estimated from the whole sample
ht_mean(s, "spend", by = "site")
#> Hajek mean by domain  (stratified design, 95% CI, t, 38 df)
#>  site  n  mean    se ci_lower ci_upper   method
#>     a 30 271.4 21.01    228.9    314.0 analytic
#>     b 10 265.7 39.27    186.2    345.2 analytic

# The difference between the two sites' means
ht_mean(s, "spend", by = "site", contrast = c(a = 1, b = -1))
#> Contrast of Hajek means  (stratified design, n = 40)
#>   contrast `a` - `b`
#>   domains  `a` 271.4333, `b` 265.7
#>   estimate 5.733333
#>   se       44.53818  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  -84.42949 to 95.89616  (t, 38 df)

# A proportion is the mean of a 0/1 variable
ht_mean(s, s$spend > 250)
#> Hajek mean  (stratified design, n = 40)
#>   estimate 0.5
#>   se       0.07207914  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  0.3580894 to 0.6419106  (logit, t, 38 df)
#>   deff     1.01  (about the same as simple random sampling)

# The share of each level of a factor, with the covariances between them
s$band <- cut(s$spend, c(0, 100, 250, 500))
shares <- ht_mean(s, "band")
shares
#> Hajek mean of `band` by level  (stratified design, 95% CI, logit, t, 38 df)
#>      level  n  mean      se ci_lower ci_upper   method
#>    (0,100] 40 0.075 0.03828  0.02585   0.1986 analytic
#>  (100,250] 40 0.425 0.07151  0.29016   0.5720 analytic
#>  (250,500] 40 0.500 0.07208  0.35809   0.6419 analytic
vcov(shares)
#>                 (0,100]     (100,250]     (250,500]
#> (0,100]    0.0014655172 -0.0006915709 -0.0007739464
#> (100,250] -0.0006915709  0.0051130268 -0.0044214559
#> (250,500] -0.0007739464 -0.0044214559  0.0051954023

# Stratified without replacement: the weights sum to N, so the two agree
all.equal(ht_mean(s, "spend", estimator = "ht")$mean, ht_mean(s, "spend")$mean)
#> [1] TRUE

# Poisson sampling has a random size, so they part company
p <- draw(pop, design_weighted("spend", n = 40, method = "poisson"),
          seed = 2, weights = TRUE)
c(hajek = ht_mean(p, "spend", variance = "none")$mean,
  ht    = ht_mean(p, "spend", "ht", variance = "none")$mean)
#>    hajek       ht 
#> 330.0012 329.5750
